items.value: Too few choices may not be a good thing, but too many can be equally difficult - the paradox of choice.
items.reasoning: The passage is built around the paradox of choice and illustrates both of its ends: Buridan's ass faced only two options and still starved, while modern people are 'overwhelmed with attractive life choices, yet find themselves unhappy and anxious'. Option D is the only one that carries this two-sided message. B merely restates the setting (uncertainty and difficult choices) without drawing the paradox out; A blames technology for weakening 'societal structure', which the passage never says (it says technology exacerbates the glut of choices); C introduces the opinion of others, which is absent from the passage.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only - a flexible environment is needed, and households need customised solutions.
items.reasoning: The passage lists the hurdles and each implied solution must answer one of them. 'Onerous bureaucracy' implies the need for a more flexible environment, so 1 holds. 'A lack of basic information about which of the myriad services and providers is best for each family' implies solutions tailored to the individual household, so 2 holds. Statement 3 fails because the passage does not mention technology of any kind - financial technology is a plausible real-world solution but not one this passage implies, which is the standard distractor in these items.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 4 only - patent pricing burdens the public's ability to buy medicines, and governments must balance patentee rights against patients' needs.
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 rests on the passage's own words: patentees set prices that 'could be unaffordable to the public', and protection 'comes at a cost, in the nature of higher prices for the patented medicine'. Assumption 4 is the unstated premise that holds the whole passage together, since it sets the patentee's legitimate return on R and D against the public's affordability problem - a trade-off only makes sense if a balance has to be struck. Assumption 2 is out because the passage says nothing about importing medicines or dependence on other countries, and 3 is out because it imports public health policy design 'in many countries', a scope the passage never touches.

items.value: Both assumptions are valid - privacy has value to the economy, and privacy is fundamentally linked to innovation.
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 follows from the opening sentence, which ties the growth of the digital economy to keeping personal data secure, and from the statement that individuals should be able to 'monetise' their data - both give privacy an economic value beyond its status as a right. Assumption 2 is stated almost directly: 'No one will innovate in a surveillance-oriented environment', and data protection laws 'should enable the right kind of innovation - one that is user-centric and privacy protecting'.

The four papers total 400 marks, so 99 per cent is 396 and the student loses exactly 4 marks in all. Writing the shortfall in each paper as d1, d2, d3, d4, we need non-negative integers with d1 + d2 + d3 + d4 = 4, and the ceiling of 100 per paper never binds because 4 is far below it. The number of such solutions is C(4 + 3, 3) = C(7, 3) = 35.

items.value: 24 different flags.
items.reasoning: Colour the stripes from top to bottom. The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours; every later stripe only has to differ from the stripe immediately above it, leaving 2 choices each time. So the count is 3 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 24. The phrase 'some or all' imposes no extra restriction, because with 4 stripes and no two adjacent alike at least two colours are used automatically, and every one of the 24 designs is therefore admissible.

items.value: 9 tiles.
items.reasoning: The floor is 400 cm by 220 cm (88000 sq cm) and each tile is 140 cm by 60 cm (8400 sq cm), so at most 10 tiles could fit by area. Nine can actually be laid, but only with a staggered arrangement rather than neat rows: standing two tiles upright at x = 0 to 60 and 60 to 120 over y = 0 to 140; laying two flat at y = 0 to 60 over x = 120 to 260 and 260 to 400; standing four upright over y = 80 to 220 at x = 140 to 200, 200 to 260, 260 to 320 and 320 to 380; and laying one flat at x = 0 to 140 over y = 140 to 200. These nine do not overlap and stay inside the floor, so the answer is 9 - note that every simple row-by-row layout stops at 8, which is the trap in this item.

items.value: 24 ways.
items.reasoning: Fill the two restricted tasks first. Task-2 must go to R or S, which is 2 choices. Task-1 cannot go to P or Q, and one of R and S has already been used on Task-2, so Task-1 has 2 candidates left (T and whichever of R and S is free). The remaining three people can take the remaining three tasks in 3! = 6 ways, giving 2 x 2 x 6 = 24.

items.value: Both statements are correct - buying 78 gm needs at least 7 coins, while weighing 78 gm on a balance needs only 4.
items.reasoning: For statement 1, only the 2 gm coin is not a multiple of 5, so the number of 2 gm coins must leave the right remainder: 78 minus 4 twos is 70, and 70 needs at least three coins (50 + 10 + 10), giving 7 in all, and no combination of 6 or fewer reaches 78. For statement 2, weighing lets you place coins on both pans, so 50 + 25 + 5 = 80 on one pan against the 78 gm object plus a 2 gm coin on the other balances with just 4 coins. The two statements are worded differently on purpose - 'buy' means the coins must add up, 'weigh' allows subtraction - and if both meant simple addition the two statements would be exact opposites, which would make options C and D impossible by construction.

items.value: Only Conclusion-2 follows: S is greater than Q.
items.reasoning: Translating the symbols: P x Q means P is greater than or equal to Q; P - T means P is less than or equal to T; T / R means T is less than R; and R +- S means R equals S. Chaining these gives Q less than or equal to P less than or equal to T, less than R, which equals S. Conclusion-2 (S greater than Q) therefore follows, since Q is at most T and T is strictly less than S. Conclusion-1 claims Q equals T, which is only one of the possibilities allowed by Q less than or equal to P less than or equal to T, so it does not follow.

items.value: Unemployment must be read as a function of rising education levels and the aspirations of young Indians.
items.reasoning: The passage's argument is that the headline unemployment rate misleads because of who it counts: younger Indians, who are better educated and 'exhibit greater willingness to wait for the right job', and it closes with 'rising education levels inflate unemployment challenges'. That is exactly option B - education and aspiration are driving the number, not simply a failing economy. A (no quality education), C (no labour-intensive industry) and D (education should produce self-employment) are all real-world claims about Indian unemployment that this passage never makes.

items.value: Statesmen need grounding in scientific method and philosophical thinking so that they see their roles, responsibilities and goals clearly.
items.reasoning: The passage's central move is the analogy 'Philosophy bears to science the same relationship which statesmanship bears to politics: movement guided by total knowledge and perspective, as against aimless and individual seeking', together with 'Government suffers, precisely like science, for lack of philosophy' and 'It is not possible to run a course aright when the goal itself has not been rightly placed'. Option A converts that directly into a practical prescription about statesmen, knowledge, perspective and goals. B imports Bacon's 'empirical statesmen' idea, which is not in this text; C widens the claim to schooling all citizens from an early age, which the passage never discusses; D drops government altogether, though government is half the passage's subject.

items.value: Liberty.
items.reasoning: The passage defines the last end of the state entirely in the language of freedom: not to dominate, not to restrain by fear, not to turn rational beings into brute beasts and machines, but to free each man from fear and to lead men 'to live by, and to exercise, a free reason'. That is liberty. Personal safety (A) and the safe functioning of body and mind (B) are named in the passage, but as the conditions the state provides so that free reason becomes possible - they are means, not the last end; communal harmony (C) is at best a by-product of men not injuring their neighbours.

items.value: The remainder is 4.
items.reasoning: Powers of 2 leave a repeating pattern on division by 6: 2, 4, 2, 4, ... - that is, remainder 2 for odd powers and 4 for even powers. Equivalently 2^192 = 4^96, and since 4 x 4 = 16 leaves remainder 4, every power of 4 leaves remainder 4. As 192 is even, the remainder is 4.

items.value: DDCA - the sequence reads ABCDD, ABCCD, ABBCD, AABCD.
items.reasoning: Break the 20 slots into four blocks of five. Each block is the string ABCD with exactly one of its letters written twice, and the doubled letter marches backwards through the alphabet from block to block. The known letters already fix block 3 as ABBCD and the tail of block 4 as ABCD, so the blocks must be ABCDD, ABCCD, ABBCD, AABCD, which fills the four gaps with D, D, C and A. None of the other options produces a consistent block pattern - C comes closest but gives ABCDC in the first block, breaking the doubling rule.

items.value: A + B + C = 6 (the numbers are 12 x 34 = 408 and 408 + 567 = 975).
items.reasoning: With E = 0 and F = 8 the product DEF is the three-digit number D08, so GHI = 975 - D08 must also be three digits with all nine letters standing for distinct digits. Trying each value of D, only D = 4 survives: DEF = 408 and GHI = 567, whose digits 4, 0, 8, 5, 6, 7 are distinct. Then AB x C4 = 408 forces AB = 12 and CD = 34, so A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 (all distinct from the rest) and A + B + C = 6. Every other value of D either repeats a digit or leaves 408's counterpart with no two-digit factorisation.

items.value: Neither conclusion follows.
items.reasoning: The false statement is 'At least one of R and S was selected', so its denial holds: neither R nor S was selected. That immediately kills conclusion 2. It also caps the total, since the only people who can have been selected are P or Q (the first true statement) and possibly T, giving at most two or three selections - never four - so conclusion 1 fails as well. The third statement, that at most two of R, S and T were selected, is then satisfied automatically and adds nothing.

items.value: Only conclusion 1 follows: if T is true then P and R cannot both be true.
items.reasoning: Suppose T is true and suppose both P and R were also true. P being true forces S to be true by rule I, and R and S both true force T to be false by rule II - a contradiction. So at least one of P and R must be false, and conclusion 1 holds. Conclusion 2 reverses rule I: the rule says P implies Q, which tells us nothing about whether Q implies P, so Q can be true while P is false and conclusion 2 does not follow.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct - there are 15 unpainted cubes, but only 4 cubes (not 6) carry exactly one blue and one green face.
items.reasoning: All six faces are painted, so the unpainted cubes form the inner block of size (7-2) x (5-2) x (3-2) = 5 x 3 x 1 = 15, making statement 1 correct. The green faces are the two 5 x 3 faces and the blue faces are the two 7 x 3 faces, so a cube touching one of each lies on one of the four edges of length 3 that run where those faces meet. Each such edge holds 3 cubes, but the two at its ends also touch a red 7 x 5 face and so have three painted faces, leaving just the middle cube of each edge - 4 cubes in all, not 6, so statement 2 is wrong.

items.value: Two positions stay unchanged - the 13th and 15th letters, both I.
items.reasoning: The word has 21 letters: five I, three E, two N, two S and one each of C, O, M, P, R, H, B, L, T. Written in reverse alphabetical order it becomes TSSRPONNMLIIIIIHEEECB, where positions 11 to 15 are the five I's. Comparing letter by letter with INCOMPREHENSIBILITIES, the original also has an I at position 13 and at position 15, and every other position differs - so exactly two positions are unchanged.
